articles.title: Icon Energy expands containership portfolio with new feeder vessel investment
articles.summary: Nasdaq-listed shipping company Icon Energy has agreed to acquire a minority interest in a company owning a 1,800 TEU ECO containership, marking a further expansion of its investments in the container shipping sector. The vessel, built in 2023, is currently employed under a fixed-rate time charter with a major...
articles.body: Nasdaq-listed shipping company Icon Energy has agreed to acquire a minority interest in a company owning a 1,800 TEU ECO containership, marking a further expansion of its investments in the container shipping sector. The vessel, built in 2023, is currently employed under a fixed-rate time charter with a major container shipping operator. The agreement provides for a daily charter rate of US$24,750, with the minimum charter period extending through February 2028. The containership is expected to generate approximately US$12 million in minimum contracted charter revenue over the remaining employment period. This amount represents revenue associated with the vessel rather than income directly attributable to Icon Energy’s proposed ownership stake. Minority investment subject to closing conditions Under the proposed transaction, Icon Energy will acquire a 2.8% minority interest in the vessel-owning company. Completion is expected by the end of October 2026, subject to the execution of definitive documentation and customary closing conditions. The company has not disclosed the financial consideration associated with the acquisition. The investment follows Icon Energy’s earlier entry into the containership segment through a 4.6% minority interest in a separate vessel-owning company. That investment involves a 2,000 TEU feeder containership built in 2008, which is employed under a time charter generating US$26,500 per day. The minimum charter period for that vessel extends through June 2028. The latest agreement would add exposure to a newer-generation feeder containership alongside the company’s existing shipping investments, although the transaction has not yet been completed.
takeaways: Nasdaq-listed shipping company Icon Energy has agreed to acquire a minority interest in a company owning a 1,800 TEU ECO containership, marking a further expansion of its investments in the container shipping sector.
The vessel, built in 2023, is currently employed under a fixed-rate time charter with a major container shipping operator.
The agreement provides for a daily charter rate of US$24,750, with the minimum charter period extending through February 2028.

articles.title: FMC proposes shipping fees and trade restrictions against Spain
articles.summary: The US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) has proposed new fees on Spanish-flagged vessels and restrictions on certain Spanish imports after concluding that Spain denied US-flagged ships access to its ports. In a statement issued on 14 October 2026, the FMC said its investigation found evidence that Spain had created...
articles.body: The US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) has proposed new fees on Spanish-flagged vessels and restrictions on certain Spanish imports after concluding that Spain denied US-flagged ships access to its ports. In a statement issued on 14 October 2026, the FMC said its investigation found evidence that Spain had created unfavorable conditions for US shipping. The regulator is now seeking public comments before deciding whether to introduce measures in response. The proposals include a $200,000 fee per voyage for all Spanish-flagged vessels and possible restrictions on imports of selected Spanish products into the United States. FMC investigation finds restrictions on US vessels The FMC launched its investigation in December 2024 following reports that Spanish authorities had refused port access to certain vessels, including ships participating in the US Maritime Administration’s Maritime Security Program. According to the Commission, its findings confirmed that Spain had denied entry to US-flagged vessels, creating unfavorable conditions for shipping in US foreign trade. The regulator said these restrictions could affect the efficiency and reliability of international maritime supply chains, while also undermining efforts to support US exports and the American merchant marine. In response, the FMC is considering two sets of measures. The first would impose a $200,000 fee on each voyage by a Spanish-flagged vessel. The second would restrict imports of certain Spanish goods. Products potentially affected include perfumes, cosmetics, oils and fats, ceramics, stone products, sugar and confectionery. articles.title: Rhenus opens humanitarian logistics office in Dubai
articles.summary: Rhenus has opened a permanent humanitarian logistics office within Dubai Humanitarian, expanding its ability to coordinate emergency relief shipments across international markets. The new office, inaugurated on 14 October 2026, brings Rhenus closer to United Nations agencies, non-governmental organisations and other...
articles.body: Rhenus has opened a permanent humanitarian logistics office within Dubai Humanitarian, expanding its ability to coordinate emergency relief shipments across international markets. The new office, inaugurated on 14 October 2026, brings Rhenus closer to United Nations agencies, non-governmental organisations and other humanitarian partners operating from the Dubai hub. The opening follows the launch of Rhenus’ humanitarian logistics services in the United Arab Emirates earlier this year. During 2026, the company also developed regional transport solutions, expanded its network of humanitarian partners and secured a licence to operate within the Dubai Humanitarian Free Zone. Supporting international relief operations From its new office, Rhenus will coordinate air, ocean and road freight shipments carrying essential supplies to areas affected by emergencies. These shipments include medical equipment, pharmaceuticals, food aid, shelter materials and emergency response supplies. The company will use its global transport network to help humanitarian organisations plan routes, secure freight capacity and manage deliveries under time-sensitive conditions. The location also allows Rhenus to work more closely with humanitarian agencies and logistics partners based within Dubai Humanitarian. “Being part of this community allows us to work more closely with our partners and better support their logistics requirements when and where they are needed,” said Hassan Alzeer, Managing Director of Rhenus Middle East. The new office brings together the company’s specialist Aid & Relief team and its wider international freight network. It also strengthens Rhenus’ presence in Dubai as the company continues developing its humanitarian logistics activities.
takeaways: Rhenus has opened a permanent humanitarian logistics office within Dubai Humanitarian, expanding its ability to coordinate emergency relief shipments across international markets.

articles.title: Suez Canal container ship transits exceed half of pre-crisis levels
articles.summary: Container ship traffic through the Suez Canal has reached its highest level since the Red Sea disruptions began, with weekly transiting capacity exceeding half of pre-crisis levels for the first time. According to BIMCO, citing Clarksons Research data, an average of 753,000 TEU of container ship capacity passed...
articles.body: Container ship traffic through the Suez Canal has reached its highest level since the Red Sea disruptions began, with weekly transiting capacity exceeding half of pre-crisis levels for the first time. According to BIMCO, citing Clarksons Research data, an average of 753,000 TEU of container ship capacity passed through the canal each week during the first two weeks of October 2026. This compares with 1.46 million TEU during the same period in 2023. The increase follows a series of decisions by major container shipping lines to restore services through the Red Sea after nearly three years of widespread diversions around the Cape of Good Hope. Shipping lines accelerate return to Suez BIMCO reported that 36% of container ship capacity travelling via either the Suez Canal or the Cape of Good Hope used the canal during the first two weeks of October. This represents a sharp increase from the average of 8% recorded between 2024 and mid-2026. However, it remains below the 80% share seen before the Red Sea attacks. The recovery began gathering pace in July 2026, when Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced the return of their AE15/SE3 Asia–Mediterranean service to the canal. Further changes followed across the Gemini Cooperation network, while members of the Ocean Alliance and Premier Alliance, along with MSC, also announced revised routings. In total, shipping lines have announced routing changes affecting 16 services since early July. The recovery has also become more balanced between sailing directions. During the third quarter, northbound capacity was equivalent to 75% of southbound capacity. That figure increased to 81% in early October. articles.title: Port of Oakland records container volume growth in September
articles.summary: The Port of Oakland handled 188,517 TEUs in September 2026, a 5.4% increase compared to September 2025, with growth in both loaded imports and exports driving the improvement. Combined loaded container volume rose 7.7% year-on-year, with loaded imports reaching 82,975 TEUs, up 9.6% and reversing declines recorded in...
articles.body: The Port of Oakland handled 188,517 TEUs in September 2026, a 5.4% increase compared to September 2025, with growth in both loaded imports and exports driving the improvement. Combined loaded container volume rose 7.7% year-on-year, with loaded imports reaching 82,975 TEUs, up 9.6% and reversing declines recorded in July and August, while loaded exports reached 63,299 TEUs, up 5.3% and marking their third consecutive month of month-on-month growth. Empty container volume of 42,243 TEUs was down 2.0 percent year-on-year. The port recorded 88 vessel calls in September, up 7.3 percent year-on-year, and total container volume increased 8.5 percent compared to August. Through the first nine months of 2026, the Port of Oakland has handled 1,656,999 TEUs, down 3.5% compared to the same period in 2025. Loaded imports are down 3.1 percent year-to-date at 706,177 TEUs, while loaded exports of 590,434 TEUs are up 0.7%. Combined loaded container volume is down 1.4% year-to-date, and empty container movements have declined 10.4 percent. Acting Director of Maritime Jason Garben described the September results as encouraging, noting growth in both import and export directions, and reaffirmed the port’s focus on delivering reliable and efficient service while working with terminal operators and ocean carriers to strengthen Oakland’s competitive position and attract additional cargo.
takeaways: The Port of Oakland handled 188,517 TEUs in September 2026, a 5.4% increase compared to September 2025, with growth in both loaded imports and exports driving the improvement.
Empty container volume of 42,243 TEUs was down 2.0 percent year-on-year.
The port recorded 88 vessel calls in September, up 7.3 percent year-on-year, and total container volume increased 8.5 percent compared to August.

articles.title: Why One Shipper Stops Paying for Air in the Caribbean Trade
articles.summary: Three years ago a hardware buyer in Port of Spain was flying in forty kilos of fasteners every other week because it felt safer than committing to a container. Then a storm shut the airport for four days and his shelves went bare while a competitor’s container was already sitting on a dock, untouched. That […]
articles.body: Three years ago a hardware buyer in Port of Spain was flying in forty kilos of fasteners every other week because it felt safer than committing to a container. Then a storm shut the airport for four days and his shelves went bare while a competitor’s container was already sitting on a dock, untouched. That competitor wasn’t smarter. They had just stopped treating a container like a gamble. Here’s the math most importers run backward. They compare the freight invoice to the air waybill, see a bigger number on the container, and walk away. What they’ve skipped is the freight paid per unit moving through the box. Once you divide the container rate by the number of cases inside it, the margin usually flips, and it flips hard in favor of the ocean move. That’s the whole case for full container load shipping in a nutshell: you’re not buying space, you’re buying the unit cost hiding behind a scary total. If your cargo is going to the Caribbean, the operator matters as much as the rate. Companies like full container load shipping specialists run fixed-day sailings into island ports where schedule slips cost real money, and a missed connection on a small lane can mean a week, not a day. What Actually Changes When You Own the Box Your freight stops sharing space with strangers. That’s the part people gloss over. With a shared load, your pallets sit next to someone else’s chemicals, someone else’s returns, someone else’s mislabeled freight that customs decides to inspect. Your cargo waits for the problem to clear even though you did nothing wrong. When you book a dedicated container, the only freight the port has to examine is yours. That alone can save a week on a lane where berth windows are tight. Dwell time is where island shipping gets expensive. A container sitting on a dock
takeaways: Three years ago a hardware buyer in Port of Spain was flying in forty kilos of fasteners every other week because it felt safer than committing to a container.
Then a storm shut the airport for four days and his shelves went bare while a competitor’s container was already sitting on a dock, untouched.
They had just stopped treating a container like a gamble.
